articles.title: Smart beds and motion sensors - is this the future of dementia care?
articles.summary: Jyoti and Bharat Patel are testing dementia technology including sensors in socks, their bed and around the house.
articles.content:
There are sensors in every room of Jyoti and Bharat Patel's home. Their movements and habits are monitored constantly.

But this doesn't worry them, in fact it gives them peace of mind.

Jyoti was diagnosed with dementia five years ago, and they are now part of an NHS trial using high-tech devices to help patients live at home safely.

The couple, who are in their 70s, are one of more than 250 families participating in the project by the UK Dementia Research Institute (UK DRI).

The hope is that the technology could be extended more widely across the health service, to reduce preventable trips to hospital and give families peace of mind.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a meaningful NHS trial using advanced sensor technology to support dementia patients living safely at home, potentially reducing hospital visits and improving quality of life for many families. It has broad significance for public health and provides detailed context about the trial and its participants.

Their home is filled with sensors, including ones in socks and their bed, which track their movements and habits. This technology helps monitor Jyoti, who was diagnosed with dementia five years ago.

**Impact** – The sensors give Jyoti and Bharat peace of mind by helping them stay safe without needing to move to a care home. More than 250 families are involved in this trial, showing that the technology could help many people live independently and reduce hospital visits.

articles.title: Ancient DNA reveals how plague kept returning for 400 years after the Black Death
articles.summary: Ancient DNA reveals that plague repeatedly returned to Europe for more than 400 years after the Black Death, evolving into new lineages and spreading through trade, migration, and war. Researchers also developed a method to date ancient plague genomes more precisely, linking many of them to specific outbreaks recorded in historical sources.
articles.content:
The Black Death is best known for the catastrophic wave of plague that swept through Europe between 1347 and 1353, killing millions of people. But the disease did not vanish once that initial disaster passed. Plague returned again and again for more than four centuries, repeatedly disrupting cities, economies, and societies across Europe and surrounding regions.

A study led by researchers at the University of Tartu is now offering a much more detailed look at what happened during those centuries. By analyzing DNA from the plague bacterium preserved in archaeological human remains, scientists were able to reconstruct how the disease spread, evolved, and repeatedly reappeared long after the Black Death.

Ancient DNA Reveals Centuries of Plague

The team reconstructed 26 genomes of Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague, from human remains recovered at 11 archaeological sites in Estonia, Russia, England, the Netherlands, and Switzerland. The samples date from the fourteenth through the eighteenth centuries, covering a large portion of the period known as the Second Plague Pandemic.

The genetic evidence suggests that plague did not simply survive in one place and repeatedly spread outward from a single source. Instead, the disease appears to have resurfaced in different parts of Europe over hundreds of years, potentially creating several new reservoirs where the bacterium could persist.

Estonia was repeatedly affected. Researchers found signs that plague entered the region multiple times during much of the Second Plague Pandemic, indicating that Estonia's connections with other parts of Europe also helped disease move across long distances.

One of the most striking patterns appeared around 1450-1500. During that period, plague lineages underwent a major expansion and split into three important branches. Those branches may have helped establish new reservoirs of Yersinia pestis in wild rodent populations.

Climate may also have influenced this expansion. The researchers point to the Great Renaissance Drought as one possible factor. Studies of modern plague systems have shown that changes in climate can strongly affect outbreaks among wild rodents, which act as natural hosts for the bacterium.

"We found evidence for repeated introductions of plague into Estonia starting already in the late 14th century and identified several previously unknown genetic lineages, both in urban and rural settings," said senior author Prof. Kristiina Tambets.

Pinpointing Ancient Plague Outbreaks

A major challenge in studying historical pandemics is figuring out exactly when ancient infections occurred.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers could follow individual variants in remarkable detail because genome sequences were usually linked to precise dates. Ancient disease samples rarely come with that kind of information. Archaeological remains are often dated using radiocarbon techniques that can produce time windows spanning many decades or even more than a century.

"With COVID-19, scientists could reconstruct the spread of individual strains extremely well because the genomes came with precise timestamps. For historical pandemics, those timestamps are often missing or may cover more than 100 years, which limits our ability to interpret the genetic data," the main author, Dr. Marcel Keller, explained.

To address that problem, the team developed a method designed to narrow those broad dating ranges. Researchers examined where individual plague genomes appeared on the bacterium's evolutionary tree and used that information to refine the likely dates of many samples.

This allowed them to place ancient infections into a much more precise historical timeline.

The researchers then applied the improved dating approach to 64 previously published plague genomes and 11 newly sequenced genomes. Their work represents the first systematic attempt to connect nearly all plague genomes currently available from the fourteenth to eighteenth centuries with outbreaks described in historical records.

"We were able to improve dating intervals for many samples, which allowed us to connect them to specific plague waves and outbreaks that were recorded in the respective towns or regions by chroniclers," said historian and corresponding author Prof. Philip Slavin.

War Helped Plague Move Across Europe

The genetic record also shows how strongly human activity influenced the spread of plague.

Newly analyzed genomes provide additional evidence linking outbreaks to the Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) and the Great Northern War (c. 1700-1721). Armies, displaced civilians, refugees, and traders frequently traveled along the same routes, creating opportunities for disease to move between regions.

"We see how Yersinia pestis splits into new branches during periods of conflict and spreads along the routes traveled by troops and displaced populations," said senior author Dr. Christiana L. Scheib.

The findings add new detail to plague outbreaks connected with the Great Northern War. During the 1710 siege of Tallinn, for example, the disease killed Swedish and Russian soldiers as well as civilians.

Taken together, the evidence shows that plague was far more than a single medieval catastrophe. It remained a recurring danger for generations, repeatedly returning to communities across Europe.

Why Plague History Still Matters

Plague is no longer a major public health threat in Europe, but Yersinia pestis has not vanished from the world. The bacterium still persists in natural rodent reservoirs in several regions.

Researchers say that understanding how plague became established after the Black Death, remained present for centuries, and eventually disappeared from Europe could help scientists better understand the long term behavior of infectious diseases.

Connecting ancient genomes with recorded outbreaks and possible animal reservoirs can reveal how diseases emerge, spread, establish themselves, and persist over long periods. That information could also improve modern disease surveillance and efforts to monitor places where plague still circulates today.

Reconstructing the Second Plague Pandemic

The project brought together researchers and evidence from several countries and scientific fields. Samples and expertise came from collaborators across Europe, including scientists at the University of Cambridge and research partners in the Netherlands and Switzerland.

By combining ancient DNA analysis, archaeology, historical records, and radiocarbon dating, the researchers produced what they describe as the most comprehensive genetic picture of the Second Plague Pandemic to date.

The findings reveal a disease that repeatedly crossed borders, evolved into new lineages, followed human movement, and continued shaping Europe for centuries after the Black Death itself had ended.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in understanding the long-term behavior of plague after the Black Death using ancient DNA analysis. This research has broad implications for infectious disease knowledge and modern disease surveillance, benefiting public health and historical epidemiology. The study is detailed, focused, and involves international collaboration, providing meaningful context and impact.
articles.personality_title: Ancient DNA shows plague returned to Europe for centuries after the Black Death
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Black Death was a deadly plague that killed millions in Europe between 1347 and 1353. But the disease did not disappear afterward. For over 400 years, plague kept coming back, affecting many cities and regions.

**What happened** – Scientists from the University of Tartu studied DNA from plague bacteria found in old human remains from several European countries. They looked at 26 plague genomes from the 14th to 18th centuries. Their work showed that plague reappeared many times in different places, not just from one original source. They also found new ways to date these plague samples more precisely by using their place on the bacteria’s family tree.

**One-sentence takeaway** – By studying ancient DNA, scientists revealed that plague returned to Europe many times after the Black Death and spread through human activity for centuries.

articles.title: Take a risk or play it safe? Neuronal tug-of-war helps the brain decide
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02911-9Using a video game involving bombs and treasure chests, researchers show how neural activity flickers between two regions of the frontal cortex when the brain weighs up a tricky decision.
articles.content:
Neurons fire up in two distinct areas of the brain ahead of a tough decision.Credit: Science Picture Co/Alamy

Some of the most rewarding decisions we make in life come with risk: do you take that job with a higher salary if it means moving to a new city and starting your life afresh? It’s an achingly tough choice. Now, researchers have observed how neuronal circuits in the human brain resolve such a dilemma in real time, revealing a ‘tug of war’ between rival neuronal groups during the moments before a decision is made.

In a study1 published in Nature Neuroscience on 15 September, researchers recorded electrical activity directly from the brains of six people. The team identified two neighbouring areas in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) — a region in the brain’s frontal lobe — that are involved with the decision-making process when risk and reward must be balanced.

The researchers found that neurons in one OFC area became more active before participants chose to pursue a reward, whereas neurons in the other OFC area became more active before they chose to avoid a risk. For tough decisions, neuronal signals rapidly flickered between the two regions before settling on a choice.

“What we found was that these two brain regions are anti-correlated in real time. So, millisecond by millisecond, when one is excited, the other is suppressed,” says study co-author Clara Starkweather, a neurosurgery resident at the University of California, San Francisco.

The findings might help researchers to better understand risk-taking and avoidant behaviour in conditions such as anxiety, obsessive–compulsive disorder, addiction and gambling disorders. “This kind of research can isolate some brain mechanisms that are related to specific symptoms” in some psychiatric conditions, says Pablo Billeke, a neurobiologist at the University of Development in Santiago, Chile.

Conflict in the cortex

The OFC is “the usual suspect for decision-making”, says Billeke. But because it is “right above the eye socket, and it sits on top of a big sheet of bone and above your sinuses and your eyes”, it is difficult to analyse in brain-imaging studies, says Starkweather.

Starkweather and her colleagues worked with six participants who had had electrodes surgically implanted in their OFC as part of an existing treatment for epilepsy or psychiatric conditions. The researchers designed a video game in which participants had to navigate through corridors lined with treasure chests and bombs. Participants had six seconds to choose whether to approach or avoid each hallway.

Some choices were a “no-brainer”, says Starkweather, such as entering a corridor featuring seven treasure chests and no bombs. But others presented the participants with an approach–avoidance conflict: would you decide to enter or avoid corridors that had an even number of each or, say, seven treasures and four bombs?
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant neuroscience breakthrough revealing how the brain makes complex risk-reward decisions by observing neuronal activity in real time. This discovery has broad implications for understanding and potentially treating psychiatric conditions like anxiety, OCD, addiction, and gambling disorders, which affect many people worldwide. The study provides detailed insights into brain mechanisms underlying decision-making, representing a meaningful advancement in health science.
articles.personality_title: Brain regions compete to help us decide on risky choices
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Making decisions that involve risk, like choosing a new job in a different city, is often difficult. Scientists wanted to understand how the brain weighs the chance of reward against the danger of loss.

**What happened** – Researchers studied six people who had electrodes placed in their brains for medical reasons. These electrodes recorded activity in two nearby areas of the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), a part of the brain involved in decision-making. While playing a video game where they had to choose whether to enter hallways with treasure chests and bombs, the participants’ brain signals flickered between these two areas. One area became more active when they leaned toward taking a risk for a reward, while the other became more active when they chose to avoid danger.

**Impact** – This is the first time scientists have seen this ‘tug of war’ happening in real time inside the human brain. Understanding how these brain regions work together helps explain why people sometimes take risks and sometimes avoid them. It also offers clues about problems like anxiety and addiction, where this decision process might not work properly.

**What's next step** – Researchers hope to study more people and explore how this brain activity changes in people with mental health conditions. This could lead to better treatments that help balance risk-taking and caution in those who struggle with these decisions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have discovered that two brain areas compete in real time to help people decide whether to take risks or play it safe, revealing how the brain balances reward and danger.
articles.personality_title_fr: Deux régions cérébrales s’affrontent pour nous aider à prendre des décisions risquées
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Prendre des décisions impliquant un risque, comme accepter un nouveau travail dans une autre ville, est souvent difficile. Des scientifiques ont voulu comprendre comment le cerveau évalue la récompense face au danger.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs ont étudié six personnes ayant des électrodes dans leur cerveau pour des raisons médicales. Ces électrodes ont enregistré l’activité dans deux zones proches du cortex orbitofrontal (COF), une partie du cerveau liée à la prise de décision. En jouant à un jeu vidéo où ils devaient choisir d’entrer dans des couloirs avec des coffres au trésor et des bombes, l’activité cérébrale des participants alternait entre ces deux zones. Une zone s’activait quand ils penchaient pour prendre un risque, l’autre quand ils préféraient éviter le danger.

**Impact** – C’est la première fois que des scientifiques observent ce « tiraillement » en temps réel dans le cerveau humain. Comprendre comment ces régions fonctionnent ensemble aide à expliquer pourquoi certaines personnes prennent des risques et d’autres non. Cela donne aussi des pistes pour mieux comprendre des troubles comme l’anxiété ou l’addiction.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent étudier plus de personnes et voir comment cette activité cérébrale change chez celles souffrant de troubles mentaux. Cela pourrait conduire à de meilleurs traitements pour équilibrer prise de risque et prudence.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Des scientifiques ont découvert que deux zones du cerveau s’affrontent en temps réel pour aider à décider de prendre des risques ou de rester prudent, révélant comment le cerveau équilibre récompense et danger.
articles.personality_title_es: Dos regiones cerebrales compiten para ayudarnos a decidir en situaciones de riesgo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Tomar decisiones que implican riesgo, como aceptar un nuevo trabajo en otra ciudad, suele ser difícil. Los científicos quisieron entender cómo el cerebro evalúa la recompensa frente al peligro.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores estudiaron a seis personas que tenían electrodos en el cerebro por razones médicas. Estos electrodos midieron la actividad en dos áreas cercanas de la corteza orbitofrontal (COF), una parte del cerebro relacionada con la toma de decisiones. Mientras jugaban un videojuego donde debían elegir si entrar en pasillos con cofres de tesoro y bombas, la actividad cerebral de los participantes cambiaba entre estas dos áreas. Una se activaba cuando preferían arriesgar para obtener una recompensa, la otra cuando preferían evitar el peligro.

**Impacto** – Es la primera vez que los científicos ven esta «lucha» en tiempo real dentro del cerebro humano. Entender cómo trabajan estas regiones ayuda a explicar por qué algunas personas toman riesgos y otras no. También da pistas para comprender problemas como la ansiedad o la adicción.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores esperan estudiar a más personas y analizar cómo cambia esta actividad cerebral en quienes tienen condiciones de salud mental. Esto podría ayudar a crear mejores tratamientos para equilibrar el riesgo y la precaución.

**Resumen en una frase** – Científicos descubrieron que dos áreas del cerebro compiten en tiempo real para ayudar a decidir si tomar riesgos o jugar a lo seguro, mostrando cómo el cerebro equilibra recompensa y peligro.
